:question/problem "A fair $5$-sided die with numbers $1$ through $5$ is rolled $9$ times. What is the probability of getting a $1$ or a $2$ exactly five times? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times that a $1$ or a $2$ is rolled. 

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=9$ rolls

- the probability of getting a $1$ or $2$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{2}{5}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(9,\frac{2}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=5$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{9}{5}){(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(1-\frac{2}{5})}^{9-5} \\  & =\frac{9!}{5!(9-5)!}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{4} \\  & =126{(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{4} \\  & =0.167\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d6e2ae69-22b8-5724-b660-3eef8661b061"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d6e2ae69-22b8-5724-b660-3eef8661b061" :answer-field/id #uuid "d6e2ae69-22b8-5724-b660-3eef8661b061" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2fce3391-052e-587a-a9de-fd2fea484deb" "answer-3301780f-7d13-59bf-babc-3915b8c2d051" "answer-eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" "answer-90225c0b-d22b-5ec7-82e0-736f61864ff1" "answer-e928e1f5-d998-5632-b572-4eff4fc046da"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2fce3391-052e-587a-a9de-fd2fea484deb" :answer/id #uuid "2fce3391-052e-587a-a9de-fd2fea484deb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.097" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3301780f-7d13-59bf-babc-3915b8c2d051" :answer/id #uuid "3301780f-7d13-59bf-babc-3915b8c2d051" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.125" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" :answer/id #uuid "eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.167" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-90225c0b-d22b-5ec7-82e0-736f61864ff1" :answer/id #uuid "90225c0b-d22b-5ec7-82e0-736f61864ff1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.184" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e928e1f5-d998-5632-b572-4eff4fc046da" :answer/id #uuid "e928e1f5-d998-5632-b572-4eff4fc046da" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.217" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106512 :question/problem "A softball team has a $70%$ chance of winning each game in a $10$-game season. What is the probability that the team wins $9$ of the $10$ games? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of games that the team wins.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=10$ games

- the probability of winning each game is $p=70%=0.7$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(10,0.7).$ We want to find the probability of winning $x=9$ games.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=9) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{9})(0.7)^{9}(1-0.7)^{10-9} \\  & =\frac{10!}{9!(10-9)!}(0.7)^{9}(0.3)^{1} \\  & =10(0.7)^{9}(0.3) \\  & =0.121\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3887d38e-9181-547d-8de9-9f160529041d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3887d38e-9181-547d-8de9-9f160529041d" :answer-field/id #uuid "3887d38e-9181-547d-8de9-9f160529041d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-692b3019-71a9-5b63-9e3c-abdf054e7e2d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-db8a2a09-b8f1-5b4e-9e51-08645ed163c6" "answer-692b3019-71a9-5b63-9e3c-abdf054e7e2d" "answer-855beeb5-4f39-591a-a8ed-3abb6b72c857" "answer-64357ced-be65-5f92-896c-49a39f578379" "answer-ceb328de-2e12-51ae-a30e-e7eea7510405"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db8a2a09-b8f1-5b4e-9e51-08645ed163c6" :answer/id #uuid "db8a2a09-b8f1-5b4e-9e51-08645ed163c6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.092" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-692b3019-71a9-5b63-9e3c-abdf054e7e2d" :answer/id #uuid "692b3019-71a9-5b63-9e3c-abdf054e7e2d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.121" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-855beeb5-4f39-591a-a8ed-3abb6b72c857" :answer/id #uuid "855beeb5-4f39-591a-a8ed-3abb6b72c857" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.159" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-64357ced-be65-5f92-896c-49a39f578379" :answer/id #uuid "64357ced-be65-5f92-896c-49a39f578379" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.257" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ceb328de-2e12-51ae-a30e-e7eea7510405" :answer/id #uuid "ceb328de-2e12-51ae-a30e-e7eea7510405" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.688" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-48a19d94-de64-5ea0-b742-40601b9c76a4" :question/id #uuid "48a19d94-de64-5ea0-b742-40601b9c76a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-331491" :question/problem "A bag contains $5$ green marbles, $7$ yellow marbles, and $8$ black marbles. {{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times a black marble is selected.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=6$ selections.

- The probability of selecting a black marble is

$$
p=\frac{8}{5+7+8}=\frac{8}{20}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(6,\frac{2}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=3$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$

\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =1-P(X>3) \\  & =1-[P(X=4)+P(X=5)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})(0.65)^{4}(0.35)^{5-4}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5})(0.65)^{5}(0.35)^{5-5}] \\  & =1-[5(0.65)^{4}(0.35)+(0.65)^{5}] \\  & =1-0.428\,415 \\  & ≈0.572,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076" :answer-field/id #uuid "82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de" :answer/id #uuid "6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.572" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107105 :tutorial/content "A **binomial distribution** is a probability distribution that models the number of successes in a sequence of $n$ independent experiments (or trials) where each outcome is either success or failure. In a binomial distribution, the probability of success in each experiment is the same.

If there are $n$ experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment, then the number of successes has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2, \ldots, n
$$

For example, if we flip a coin $5$ times, then the number of heads follows a binomial distribution.

- Each toss is an experiment that either results in success (i.e., heads) or failure (i.e., tails).

- There are $n=5$ experiments.

- Each experiment has a probability $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$ of success.

So, the number of heads has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(1-\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

When a random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution consisting of $n$ experiments (or trials) and the probability of success on each trial is $p,$ we often write

$$
X\sim B(n,p).
$$

 

In words, we say, "the random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution with $n$ trials and probability $p$ of success on each trial."" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106014 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

:question/problem "A fair $5$-sided die with numbers $1$ through $5$ is rolled $9$ times. What is the probability of getting a $1$ or a $2$ exactly five times? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times that a $1$ or a $2$ is rolled. 

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=9$ rolls

- the probability of getting a $1$ or $2$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{2}{5}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(9,\frac{2}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=5$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{9}{5}){(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(1-\frac{2}{5})}^{9-5} \\  & =\frac{9!}{5!(9-5)!}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{4} \\  & =126{(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{4} \\  & =0.167\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d6e2ae69-22b8-5724-b660-3eef8661b061"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d6e2ae69-22b8-5724-b660-3eef8661b061" :answer-field/id #uuid "d6e2ae69-22b8-5724-b660-3eef8661b061" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2fce3391-052e-587a-a9de-fd2fea484deb" "answer-3301780f-7d13-59bf-babc-3915b8c2d051" "answer-eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" "answer-90225c0b-d22b-5ec7-82e0-736f61864ff1" "answer-e928e1f5-d998-5632-b572-4eff4fc046da"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2fce3391-052e-587a-a9de-fd2fea484deb" :answer/id #uuid "2fce3391-052e-587a-a9de-fd2fea484deb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.097" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3301780f-7d13-59bf-babc-3915b8c2d051" :answer/id #uuid "3301780f-7d13-59bf-babc-3915b8c2d051" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.125" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" :answer/id #uuid "eff5311f-f548-5e70-829c-1a093a0352eb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.167" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-90225c0b-d22b-5ec7-82e0-736f61864ff1" :answer/id #uuid "90225c0b-d22b-5ec7-82e0-736f61864ff1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.184" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e928e1f5-d998-5632-b572-4eff4fc046da" :answer/id #uuid "e928e1f5-d998-5632-b572-4eff4fc046da" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.217" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106512 :question/problem "A softball team has a $70%$ chance of winning each game in a $10$-game season. What is the probability that the team wins $9$ of the $10$ games? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of games that the team wins.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=10$ games

- the probability of winning each game is $p=70%=0.7$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(10,0.7).$ We want to find the probability of winning $x=9$ games.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$

In a binomial distribution, the probability of success in each experiment is the same.

If there are $n$ experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment, then the number of successes has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2, \ldots, n
$$

For example, if we flip a coin $5$ times, then the number of heads follows a binomial distribution.

- Each toss is an experiment that either results in success (i.e., heads) or failure (i.e., tails).

- There are $n=5$ experiments.

- Each experiment has a probability $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$ of success.

So, the number of heads has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(1-\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

When a random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution consisting of $n$ experiments (or trials) and the probability of success on each trial is $p,$ we often write

$$
X\sim B(n,p).
$$

 

In words, we say, "the random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution with $n$ trials and probability $p$ of success on each trial."" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106014 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-8dd54609-ae0c-53a9-a2a1-7823f9aa6595" :question/id #uuid "8dd54609-ae0c-53a9-a2a1-7823f9aa6595"] ["question-8dd54609-ae0c-53a9-a2a1-7823f9aa6595" :question/math-academy-id "q-84747"] ["question-8dd54609-ae0c-53a9-a2a1-7823f9aa6595" :question/problem "Which of the following random variables could be modeled as a binomial distribution?

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=9$ rolls

- the probability of getting a $1$ or $2$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{2}{5}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(9,\frac{2}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=5$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{9}{5}){(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(1-\frac{2}{5})}^{9-5} \\  & =\frac{9!}{5!(9-5)!}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{4} \\  & =126{(\frac{2}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{4} \\  & =0.167\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=7$ shots.

- The probability of success is $p=50%=0.5.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(7,0.5).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.5)^{x}(1-0.5)^{7-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.5)^{x}(0.5)^{7-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that $3$ or fewer of the $7$ shots are successful. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & ={\sum }_{x=0}^{3}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.5)^{7} \\  & =[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{0})+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{1})+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{3})](0.5)^{7} \\  & =(1+7+21+35)\cdot \frac{1}{128} \\  & =64\cdot \frac{1}{128} \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ec42c1b6-69ea-5d9d-b8b5-5ad8c82e5789" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-e6dd545c-98d8-56db-ace2-b43058497897" :answer-field/id #uuid "e6dd545c-98d8-56db-ace2-b43058497897"] ["answer-18ce8a43-15dd-5064-88bf-0a2b654ec3d7" :answer/id #uuid "18ce8a43-15dd-5064-88bf-0a2b654ec3d7"] ["answer-18ce8a43-15dd-5064-88bf-0a2b654ec3d7" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-18ce8a43-15dd-5064-88bf-0a2b654ec3d7" :answer/value "0.5"] ["answer-field-e6dd545c-98d8-56db-ace2-b43058497897" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-e6dd545c-98d8-56db-ace2-b43058497897" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-e6dd545c-98d8-56db-ace2-b43058497897" :answer-field/correct "answer-18ce8a43-15dd-5064-88bf-0a2b654ec3d7"] ["answer-field-e6dd545c-98d8-56db-ace2-b43058497897" :answer-field/choices "answer-18ce8a43-15dd-5064-88bf-0a2b654ec3d7"] ["question-ec42c1b6-69ea-5d9d-b8b5-5ad8c82e5789" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-e6dd545c-98d8-56db-ace2-b43058497897"] [17592186105826 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ec42c1b6-69ea-5d9d-b8b5-5ad8c82e5789"] ["question-f0df1382-8e7a-5174-b609-3e041c2744d5" :question/id #uuid "f0df1382-8e7a-5174-b609-3e041c2744d5"] ["question-f0df1382-8e7a-5174-b609-3e041c2744d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-84797"] ["question-f0df1382-8e7a-5174-b609-3e041c2744d5" :question/problem "On a particular webpage, there is an $80%$ probability that each downloaded file does not contain a computer virus. Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=6$ members

- since $70%$ of union members are in favor of the change, the probability of selecting a member in favor of the change is $p=70%=0.7$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(6,0.7).$

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){(0.7)}^{x}{(1-0.7)}^{6-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){(0.7)}^{x}{(0.3)}^{6-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at most two members are in favor of the changed conditions. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{0}){(0.7)}^{0}{(0.3)}^{6-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{1}){(0.7)}^{1}{(0.3)}^{6-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{2}){(0.7)}^{2}{(0.3)}^{6-2} \\  & =1{(0.7)}^{0}{(0.3)}^{6}+6{(0.7)}^{1}{(0.3)}^{5}+15{(0.7)}^{2}{(0.3)}^{4} \\  & ≈0.070\end{aligned}
$$

You may assume that the bag contains a large number of candies and that the probability of selecting a red candy is the same on each trial."] ["question-7a3cf3a8-b182-51ac-8e52-79ae8f41f3ac" :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of red candies.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=16$ candies

- the probability of getting a red candy is $p=70%=0.7$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(16,0.7).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{16}{x})(0.7)^{x}(1-0.7)^{16-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{16}{x})(0.7)^{x}(0.3)^{16-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that fewer than $15$ candies are red. This corresponds to $P(X<15).$

However, computing

$$
P(X<15)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+…+P(X=14)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<15) & =1-P(X\ge 15) \\  & =1-[P(X=15)+P(X=16)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{16}{15})(0.7)^{15}(0.3)^{16-15}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{16}{16})(0.7)^{16}(0.3)^{16-16}] \\  & =1-[16(0.7)^{15}(0.3)+(0.7)^{16}] \\  & =1-0.026\,112 \\  & =0.974\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-7a3cf3a8-b182-51ac-8e52-79ae8f41f3ac" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a3e2700b-68a3-5d33-878c-99b41a013f77" :answer-field/id ["question-cfd01f57-c0cd-576d-bb6c-c4a4c9533c2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-131048"] ["question-cfd01f57-c0cd-576d-bb6c-c4a4c9533c2d" :question/problem "A box of chocolates contains cherry creams and almond little cakes in the ratio of $3:2.$ Ten chocolates are selected at random, with replacement. What is the probability of getting at most $9$ cherry creams? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-cfd01f57-c0cd-576d-bb6c-c4a4c9533c2d" :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be the number of selected cherry creams.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=10$ selected chocolates

- since cherry creams and almond little cakes are in the ratio of $3:2,$ the probability of selecting a cherry cream from the box is $p=\frac{3}{5}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(10,\frac{3}{5}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{x}){(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}{(1-\frac{3}{5})}^{10-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{x}){(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{10-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of getting at most $9$ cherry creams. This corresponds to $P(X\le 9).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\le 9)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+…+P(X=9)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 9) & =1-P(X>9) \\  & =1-P(X=10) \\  & =1-(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{10}{10}){(\frac{3}{5})}^{10}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{10-10} \\  & =1-1{(\frac{3}{5})}^{10}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{0} \\  & =1-0.006\,047 \\  & ≈0.994\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-cfd01f57-c0cd-576d-bb6c-c4a4c9533c2d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-5d275997-d198-54d6-a316-0c412fd339be" :answer-field/id Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=25$ students in the class

- the probability of selecting a student having the flu next week is $0.3$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(25,0.3).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{25}{x})(0.3)^{x}(1-0.3)^{25-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{25}{x})(0.3)^{x}(0.7)^{25-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that two or more students from the class will have the flu next week. This corresponds to $P(X\ge 2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=25)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{25}{0})(0.3)^{0}(0.7)^{25-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{25}{1})(0.3)^{1}(0.7)^{25-1}] \\  & =1-[(0.3)^{0}(0.7)^{25}+25(0.3)^{1}(0.7)^{24}] \\  & =1-0.001\,571 \\  & ≈0.998\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=6$ tested bulbs

- the probability of choosing a defective bulb is $p=5%=0.05$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(6,0.05).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.05)^{x}(1-0.05)^{6-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.05)^{x}(0.95)^{6-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at least two bulbs are defective. This corresponds to $P(X\ge 2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\ge 2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)+…+P(X=6)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{0})(0.05)^{0}(0.95)^{6-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{1})(0.05)^{1}(0.95)^{6-1}] \\  & =1-[1(0.05)^{0}(0.95)^{6}+6(0.05)^{1}(0.95)^{5}] \\  & =1-0.967\,226 \\  & ≈0.033\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=5$ deliveries.

- The probability of success is $p=65%=0.65.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,0.65).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.65)^{x}(1-0.65)^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.65)^{x}(0.35)^{5-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that the drone succeeds at most $3$ times. This corresponds to $P(X\le 3).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\le 3)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+…+P(X=3),
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =1-P(X>3) \\  & =1-[P(X=4)+P(X=5)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})(0.65)^{4}(0.35)^{5-4}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5})(0.65)^{5}(0.35)^{5-5}] \\  & =1-[5(0.65)^{4}(0.35)+(0.65)^{5}] \\  & =1-0.428\,415 \\  & ≈0.572,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-a48cf853-bbc5-5226-99de-0617e7d6b622" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076" :answer-field/id #uuid "82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076"] ["answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de" :answer/id #uuid "6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de"] ["answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de" :answer/value "0.572"] ["answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076" :answer-field/correct "answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de"] ["answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076" :answer-field/choices "answer-6b2e490a-1bb1-5990-9e77-13fbe35019de"] ["question-a48cf853-bbc5-5226-99de-0617e7d6b622" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-82a882d2-167d-5383-9684-88e207eea076"] [17592186105830 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a48cf853-bbc5-5226-99de-0617e7d6b622"] [17592186107105 :tutorial/content "A **binomial distribution** is a probability distribution that models the number of successes in a sequence of $n$ independent experiments (or trials) where each outcome is either success or failure. Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of students that passed the exam.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=5$ students

- the probability that each student passed the exam is $p=75\%=0.75$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(5,0.75).$ We want to find the probability that $x=3$ of the students passed the exam.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3})(0.75)^{3}(1-0.75)^{5-3} \\  & =\frac{5!}{3!(5-3)!}(0.75)^{3}(0.25)^{2} \\  & =10(0.75)^{3}(0.25)^{2} \\  & =0.264\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186106512 :question/id #uuid "7bd6c9ff-00f9-5185-b985-9d9007df87dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-84050" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105825 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6b8cf2b4-0b4f-513b-a5dc-f582c973e098" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Probability of a Binomial Random Variable for Some Value"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a3b70e6c-57cb-5df5-9660-163b11755683" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.159" :db/id 17592186105221} {:answer/id #uuid "ce36c17a-038d-576e-8e33-ff32227e998d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.257" :db/id 17592186105222} {:answer/id #uuid "100c026d-f05b-5aa4-9711-3cc3ac9b5eec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.092" :db/id 17592186105223} {:answer/id #uuid "4a3d6bbd-1871-5d55-8d51-96e54c8a82ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.688" :db/id 17592186105224} {:answer/id #uuid "78494c48-24d8-59e5-925d-f6938421fa76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.121" :db/id 17592186105225}] :answer-field/id #uuid "329b62cb-c9ff-58c9-b520-1cfc155601f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186105220}] :question/problem "A softball team has a $70%$ chance of winning each game in a $10$-game season. 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A spinner with three regions is designed so that the probability it lands on red is $\frac{3}{10},$ the probability it lands on blue is $\frac{2}{5},$ and on green $\frac{3}{10}.$ What is the probability that the spinner lands on red or green exactly $5$ times if it is spun $12$ times? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the spinner lands on red or green.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=12$ spins

- the probability of landing on red or green on any spin is

$$
p=\frac{3}{10}+\frac{3}{10}=\frac{3}{5}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,\frac{3}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=5$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{5}){(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(1-\frac{3}{5})}^{12-5} \\  & =\frac{12!}{5!(12-5)!}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{7} \\  & =792{(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{7} \\  & =0.101\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186105826 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105660 :question/id #uuid "cbc5bcb5-2c64-5895-ba1c-cc6d86207667" :question/math-academy-id "e-7393"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ce428740-1268-5071-9a45-69cdc07aea64" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106514 :question/id #uuid "8fa71935-4c6e-5d50-a448-06f78935710a" :question/math-academy-id "q-84149"} {:db/id 17592186106515 :question/id #uuid "29eb532e-8969-5f9d-b0f7-5a7f9950e1c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-84152"} {:db/id 17592186265934 :question/id #uuid "ff4846a3-1ee2-540e-bb35-379cc2eedb30" :question/math-academy-id "q-130573"} {:db/id 17592186265969 :question/id #uuid "c94e54ed-d2e7-59bc-a8f2-2b0febd9e006" :question/math-academy-id "q-130744"} {:db/id 17592186265970 :question/id #uuid "d0bf184d-d7ca-56cb-ba56-14f65e4f1f16" :question/math-academy-id "q-130746"} {:db/id 17592186304923 :question/id #uuid "64469c0a-c9a4-5634-8d45-1147a1381d27" :question/math-academy-id "q-331526"} {:db/id 17592186354340 :question/id #uuid "fac74754-68c7-525c-973a-4d985a07fcb5" :question/math-academy-id "q-84787"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Probability of a Binomial Random Variable Over an Interval"} {:db/id 17592186105660 :question/id #uuid "cbc5bcb5-2c64-5895-ba1c-cc6d86207667" :question/math-academy-id "e-7393" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186105826 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ce428740-1268-5071-9a45-69cdc07aea64" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Probability of a Binomial Random Variable Over an Interval"}] :question/problem "A standard fair die is rolled $8$ times. Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times we get an even number.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=8$ rolls

- the probability of rolling an even number on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\dfrac{3}{6} = 0.5
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(8,0.5).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{x})(0.5)^{x}(1-0.5)^{8-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{x})(0.5)^{x}(0.5)^{8-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of rolling an even number at least $7$ times. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 7) & =P(X=7)+P(X=8) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{7})(0.5)^{7}(0.5)^{8-7}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{8})(0.5)^{8}(0.5)^{8-8} \\  & =8(0.5)^{7}(0.5)+1(0.5)^{8} \\  & =0.035\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186106514 :question/id #uuid "8fa71935-4c6e-5d50-a448-06f78935710a" :question/math-academy-id "q-84149"} {:db/id 17592186106515 :question/id #uuid - The number of questions answered correctly by a student in a $12$-question exam

- The heights of $10$ elementary school children" :question/worked-solution "A binomial distribution models the number of successes in a sequence of $n$ independent experiments (where each outcome is either success or failure).

- Random variable II could be modeled as a binomial distribution. The number of questions answered in a $12$- question exam can be interpreted as the number of successes in a sequence of $12$ independent experiments.

- Random variable III could *not* be modeled as a binomial distribution. The heights cannot be interpreted as "success" or "failure."

If the player plays $12$ games, what is the probability that he wins at least $2$ of the games? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of games that the player wins.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=12$ games

- the probability of winning each game is $p=40\%=0.4$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(12,0.4).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{x})(0.4)^{x}(1-0.4)^{12-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{x})(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{12-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that the player wins at least 2 of the games. This corresponds to $P(X \geq 2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X \geq 2) = P(X=2) + P(X=3) + \ldots + P(X=12)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{0})(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{12-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{1})(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{12-1}] \\  & =1-[(0.6)^{12}+12(0.4)(0.6)^{11}] \\  & =1-0.019\,591 \\  & =0.980\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186106516 :question/id #uuid "89d84ad1-9c54-50de-b286-c51160255480" :question/math-academy-id "q-84153"} {:db/id 17592186106517 :question/id #uuid "2e6311d2-17da-5bd4-a8bb-025d853635b4" :step/math-academy-id 27401 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106776}} {:db/id 17592186106771 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107105 :tutorial/content "A **binomial distribution** is a probability distribution that models the number of successes in a sequence of $n$ independent experiments (or trials) where each outcome is either success or failure. In a binomial distribution, the probability of success in each experiment is the same.

If there are $n$ experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment, then the number of successes has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2, \ldots, n
$$

For example, if we flip a coin $5$ times, then the number of heads follows a binomial distribution.

- Each toss is an experiment that either results in success (i.e., heads) or failure (i.e., tails).

- There are $n=5$ experiments.

- Each experiment has a probability $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$ of success.

So, the number of heads has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(\frac{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(1-\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x} \\  & =(\frac{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5-x} \\  & =(\frac{5}{x}){(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

When a random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution consisting of $n$ experiments (or trials) and the probability of success on each trial is $p,$ we often write

$$
X\sim B(n,p).
$$

 

In words, we say, "the random variable $X$ follows a binomial distribution with $n$ trials and probability $p$ of success on each trial."" :tutorial/id #uuid "7e7bad04-ccb9-574b-9792-eb4b8a51b62b" 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.

$$

17592186045417] [17592186357392 1071 "Which of the following random variables could be modeled as a binomial distribution?

- there are $n=12$ spins

$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,\frac{3}{5}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=5$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

\begin{aligned}P(X=5) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{12}{5}){(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(1-\frac{3}{5})}^{12-5} \\  & =\frac{12!}{5!(12-5)!}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{7} \\  & =792{(\frac{3}{5})}^{5}{(\frac{2}{5})}^{7} \\  & =0.101\end{aligned}
$$
